summary: Defines semantics for the Session Description Protocol that tie a Forward Error Correction stream to the media streams it protects, using the media line grouping mechanism of RFC 3388. It was replaced by RFC 5956.

eli5.summary: Sometimes a video sends extra repair data in case pieces get lost. This note says how to label which repair stream goes with which video stream. It was later replaced.

subtitle: How to label repair streams that protect media in a session description.

tldr.problem: When Forward Error Correction repair streams are sent alongside media streams in a session, there is no standard way to indicate which repair stream protects which media stream.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4756 defines FEC grouping semantics that extend RFC 3388 (media line grouping) to allow SDP to group FEC repair streams with the media streams they protect using the group attribute.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can now unambiguously associate repair data with the media it protects, enabling robust transmission over loss-prone networks. RFC 5956 later superseded this specification.

facts.label: Protection modes
facts.value: One FEC protects multiple payloads, or one payload has multiple FEC streams

today: RFC 4756 defined FEC grouping semantics for SDP, but it was superseded by RFC 5956, which provides updated procedures and requirements. For new implementations, RFC 5956 is the authoritative specification.

sections.title: Forward Error Correction in Streaming Media
sections.content:
Forward Error Correction (FEC) is a technique that adds redundancy to transmitted data so receivers can recover lost information without asking for a retransmit. In streaming media carried by RTP over IP, FEC is particularly valuable because retransmission delays are unacceptable; the original data must arrive in time or be discarded.

FEC works by computing extra information from the original data such that if some of the original is lost, the receiver can reconstruct it from what arrives plus the extra information. Compared to retransmission, FEC trades bandwidth (sending extra data) for latency (no round-trip delays).
sections.eli5: Imagine sending a video, then sending a backup copy of key frames. If a frame gets lost, the backup can fill in the gap. You send extra data instead of asking for a resend.

sections.title: Separate FEC Streams and the Need for Grouping
sections.content:
FEC can be sent in two ways: multiplexed with the original stream (mixed into the same RTP stream) or as a separate stream. When FEC is separate, the session description must clearly state which FEC stream protects which media streams.

RFC 3388 provides a general mechanism for grouping related media lines in an SDP session description. RFC 4756 builds on this, defining the FEC semantics: a group with the attribute a=group:FEC associates payload streams (the original media) with FEC streams (the repair data). The group lists the media line identifiers (mid values) of all streams in the association.
sections.eli5: If you send video and backup separately, the description needs to say 'this backup protects that video.' That's what FEC grouping does.

sections.title: FEC Group Semantics and Flexibility
sections.content:
A FEC group is flexible: one FEC stream may protect multiple payload streams (for example, a single repair stream protecting both audio and video), or one payload stream may be protected by multiple FEC streams (for redundant repair at different levels). The group attribute simply states the association; the detailed protection scheme and parameters are conveyed by the specific FEC algorithm in use.

For example, an SDP might contain: a video stream (mid:3), a video FEC stream (mid:4), and a group stating a=group:FEC 3 4. This tells endpoints that stream 4 protects stream 3. Both streams can then use the same network address and port, or different ones; the SDP will specify the address and port for each.
sections.eli5: You can say one backup protects multiple streams, or one stream has multiple backups. The description just lists which protection goes with which media.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Status
sections.content:
When a node does not understand FEC grouping, it can take one of two approaches: ignore the group attributes and operate without FEC support, or reject the entire session. The RFC recommends that implementations support both options, allowing graceful fallback to FEC-less operation when needed.

RFC 4756 updated RFC 3720 to allow iSCSI extension items to be defined by standards track RFCs, not only informational RFCs. However, RFC 4756 was itself superseded by RFC 5956, which provides clarified procedures and updated requirements. The newer RFC is now the authoritative specification for FEC grouping in SDP.
sections.eli5: If a system doesn't know about FEC grouping, it can either skip it and play the video anyway, or refuse the whole session. Either way, things still work. A newer RFC fixed this later.
